newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: FOCUS-Malaysia rushes to rescue roiling markets.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Malaysia rushes to rescue roiling markets.

text.p: Malaysian authorities swept in on Friday to help steady stock and currency markets pummelled by foreign selling and speculation, but the support will not erase near-term uncertainties, analysts said.
Kuala Lumpur stock prices have dropped all week, culminating in a nearly three percent tumble on Thursday on fears that Thailand's economic slowdown will spread to the region.

But, helped by local and government-backed funds seeking bargains, the Composite Index of leading blue chips recouped more than two percent in morning losses to end up 0.64 points to 1,041.91 on Friday. For the week, it lost 5.91 percent.
Dealers said there was talk the national Employees Provident Fund and government investment arm Permodalan Nasional Bhd came in to pick up Malaysian stocks.
It was also a rocky week for the ringgit, which was first overpowered by a strengthening yen and later by offshore speculative selling.
The ringgit rallied on Friday and was quoted at 2.4880/90 at 0900 GMT in Kuala Lumpur against 2.5065/75 on Thursday.
Bank Negara Malaysia, the central bank, issued a rare public statement on Friday to deny rumours it had told banks to stop ringgit swap facilities for foreign banks.

It said the shortage in the ringgit from "speculative activities" had caused a spike in short-term money rates. Earlier on Friday, the overnight interbank rate traded at 15 to 20 percent from 8.5 percent on Thursday.

Bank Negara has been especially on guard against weakness in the ringgit after talk of a possible baht devaluation sent the Thai currency reeling and brought in concerted central bank support, analysts said.
Despite the Malaysian central bank's denial about locking out offshore swap facilities, dealers said they believed such a freeze was being done to stamp out speculators.

"I wouldn't be surprised at all if they (Bank Negara) were doing what the Bank of Thailand did to break links between onshore and offshore (banks) to scare speculators. It does the job very quickly," Dave Carbon, market strategist at Pacific Asset Management in Singapore, said.

Analysts also saw an official Malaysian hand in the unexpectedly early release of official data, showing a surprising 1.75 billion ringgit ($700 million) trade surplus in March. That figure surpassed market expectations.
Trade data is usually issued towards the end of the month.
The government was also able to hand out another bit of good economic news, announcing retail inflation in April was 2.6 percent, the lowest rate for several years.
The inflation report had been anticipated on Friday.
"It's very coincidental, isn't it?" remarked an equity market analyst at a foreign brokerage in Malaysia.
A stock market analyst at a domestic firm said: "It's quite a strategic release. I think they (the government) are trying to comfort the market."

While some order in the markets had been restored, analysts said battered investor sentiment may take a while to heal. "I think basically the mood will be one of caution," said Andy Tan, economist at MMS International.

Shaken by the property crisis in Thailand and jittery about measures to quell property speculation by authorities in Singapore, the Philippines and Malaysia, foreign funds have been taking some money out of Asian stocks, analysts said.

In Thailand, the composite SET Index lost 44.24 points, or 7.3 percent, this week after falling 54.67 points, or 8.3 percent, a week earlier. Manila stocks fell 54.96 points on Friday, closing at a year-low of 2,576.13.

"It's a confidence game," said Lai Tak Heong, research director at Socgen-Crosby. "If the market goes down lower, it may have a spillover to the economy. People may hold back from purchasing consumer durables.
"Right now, the markets are very sentiment-driven," he added. ($1 = 2.5 ringgit)
-- Kuala Lumpur newsroom 603-201-4813
